rows.text: 6 January 1861 order exempted Colegio de Niñas de San Ignacio from nationalization; dissolved Cofradía de Aránzazu's patronage passed to civic board headed by Ignacio Jaynaga.
Before February law, Juárez commissioned Luis Garrone and Juan Navarro to inspect Divino Salvador and San Hipólito hospitals' condition and funds.
Dirección General de Beneficencia Pública founded 28 February 1861; disputes with Ayuntamiento over Tecpam de Santiago, Hospicio de Pobres, Casa de Corrección, Niños Expósitos.
1861 Directorate regulations assigned child vaccination, foundling care, institutional assistance, and work for beggars; semiannual staff meetings and budget oversight were prescribed.
12 April 1861 Ayuntamiento protested federal takeover of charitable powers and retained spending obligations; urged abolition of federal Directorate arrangement.
December 1861 compromise assigned care contributions to both Directorate and city council; April 1862 complaints said central salaries diverted money needed by Hospital San Pablo.
Government abolished Dirección General de Beneficencia Pública on 30 Aug 1862; notice returned welfare institutions to district municipalities amid fiscal and war pressures.
Jan 1865 capital budget projected 1,171,767.45 pesos in costs versus 683,086 income; planned 73,784 for San Andrés; 39,120 San Pablo; 71,992 Hospicio de Pobres; other named hospitals.
Sept 1865 Consejo General de Beneficencia chaired by Carlota announced government approval of 20,000-peso credit for institutions, to allocate by needs.
After Jesuit expulsion, an epidemic prompted bishop’s request for 400-bed hospital at San Andrés site in 1769; in 1783 government turned it over for archiepiscopal management.
San Andrés held Maximilian's body for embalming in 1867; former chapel was destroyed in 1868 and Xicoténcatl street cut through, in historian's account.
1904 San Andrés demolition on Tacuba; Contri Communications Palace started 1905 with named foreign contractors; occupied under Madero 1912; MUNAL opened 1982.
Official CDMX heritage guide attributes survival of Hospital de Jesús amid Reform to secular foundation; León Garduño lists Hospital de Jesús among privately administered 1861 establishments.

1428 is the standard shorthand for a Triple Alliance of Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan, but its political formation around the Tepanec war should be presented as a process, not an uncontested single-day event.
The Templo Mayor was enlarged repeatedly; its two principal shrines were Tláloc on the north and Huitzilopochtli on the south.

López Luján describes a dismembered Coyolxauhqui relief from stage IVa-1, earlier than the better-known monolithic disk associated with stage IVb, occupying a corresponding position beneath the southern shrine.
The Coyolxauhqui stone uncovered in February 1978 prompted the archaeological project, while the interpretive connection to the Coatepec story depends on iconography and ritual contextual arguments.

INAH reports destruction of the Templo Mayor following the defeat of 13 August 1521, with colonial houses erected over its former site. Surviving lower stages are not the intact exterior seen in 1519.
INAH identifies an approximately 1900 brick water collector under the modern walkway, with a trench cutting through the ancient temple construction stages across a strip about two metres wide.
INAH dates discovery by electric-company workers of Coyolxauhqui to 21 February 1978 and names Eduardo Matos Moctezuma as founder of Proyecto Templo Mayor.

INAH credits Manuel Gamio with uncovering the southwest temple corner in 1914; its English guide dates the site museum opening to 12 October 1987. The 1978 find was not the first archaeological indication of the Templo Mayor.

Mario Camarena describes the 1900 inauguration of an electric tram line serving Tacubaya, linking the old core of Mexico City with western settlements; the same abstract discusses drainage and lighting changes.
INAH dates the start of animal-drawn tram service in Tlalpan to 1891 and describes a 1900 electric tram connection from the Zócalo to San Fernando.
UNAM CCH's teaching material reports an area of 8.5 square kilometres for Mexico City in 1858 and 40.5 in 1910; their underlying boundary and measurement definitions have not yet been validated.

INEHRM describes the Decena Trágica as the February 9–23, 1913 Mexico City upheaval in which Victoriano Huerta's military coup overthrew President Francisco I. Madero and Vice President José María Pino Suárez.

INAH describes the main San Francisco church's 1861 closure, dismantling of some altarpieces, tribunes and choir furnishings, transfer of paintings to the Academy of Fine Arts, and destruction or division of convent spaces.

The INAH monument catalogue describes the post-Reform transfer of the San Francisco church to an Episcopal Protestant congregation, its sale to the Jesuits on June 21, 1898, and Franciscan return around 1948.

An official reconstruction directive reproduced in a UNAM-published 1986 documentary abstract states that reconstruction work at the Nonoalco-Tlatelolco housing complex would not be conditional on changes to residents' existing property regime.
The same official Tlatelolco reconstruction directive envisaged paying rebuilding costs from insurance proceeds and congressionally approved reconstruction resources.

Rabell and Mier y Terán's 1986 abstract juxtaposes 3,745 damaged residential buildings, about 90,000 affected dwellings (30,000 requiring demolition), and 46,000 families needing assistance from different agencies; these refer to different units and measurement scopes.

Lucía Álvarez Mosso's December 1985 abstract describes low wages, long hours and intense production demands in garment work, and discusses workplace closures and insecure employment after the September earthquakes.

In a 2018 journal abstract, Eugenia Allier Montaño reports that the September 2017 national press frequently compared the 2017 earthquake with 1985, discussing rescue volunteers, affected areas and government actions.
